Suppose we have the second-order homogeneous boundary value (BVP) problem

$$
{y}^{″}(x)+P(x){y}^{′}+Q(x)y=0,\,a\le x\le b
$$

with the Robin (mixed) boundary conditions

$$
{\alpha }_{1}y(a)+{\beta }_{1}{y}^{′}(a)=0,\,{\alpha }_{2}y(b)+{\beta }_{2}{y}^{′}(b)=0
$$

where $P$ and $Q$ are continuous on $[a,b],$ and ${\alpha }_{i}$ and ${\beta }_{i}$ are real constants such that $({\alpha }_{i},{\beta }_{i})\ne (0,0).$ Furthermore, suppose the fundamental solutions to the equation are ${y}_{1}(x)$ and ${y}_{2}(x).$ 

Now, let's define the following matrix:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}\,{\alpha }_{1}{y}_{1}(a)+{\beta }_{1}{y}_{1}^{′}(a) & {\alpha }_{1}{y}_{2}(a)+{\beta }_{1}{y}_{2}^{′}(a) \\ {\alpha }_{2}{y}_{1}(b)+{\beta }_{2}{y}_{1}^{′}(b) & {\alpha }_{2}{y}_{2}(b)+{\beta }_{2}{y}_{2}^{′}(b)\end{aligned}]
$$

Then, the BVP has a unique, trivial solution $y≡0$ if and only if $det(A)\ne 0.$

In other words, if the determinant equals zero, then the BVP has *infinitely many solutions*.

Notice that, in our case, we have Neumann boundary conditions. So, setting ${\alpha }_{i}=0,{\beta }_{i}=1,a=0,$ and $b=\pi ,$ the matrix $A$ reduces to

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}{y}_{1}^{′}(0) & {y}_{2}^{′}(0) \\ {y}_{1}^{′}(\pi ) & {y}_{2}^{′}(\pi )\end{aligned}].
$$

To find the fundamental solutions, we set $y={e}^{mx}.$ The auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}^{2}+4 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have $m=\pm 2\text{i}.$ So, the fundamental solutions are 

$$
{y}_{1}(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡2x\text{ and }{y}_{2}(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡2x.
$$

Differentiating, we have

$$
{y}_{1}^{′}(x)=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2x,\,{y}_{2}^{′}(x)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡2x.
$$

Therefore, the matrix $A$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =[\begin{aligned}-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot 0) & 2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\cdot 0) \\ -2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot \pi ) & 2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\cdot \pi )\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

and we have

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =0\cdot 2-2\cdot 0 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $det(A)=0$ we conclude that this BVP $\text{has infinitely many solutions}.$

Suppose we have the second-order homogeneous boundary value (BVP) problem

y″(x)+P(x)y′+Q(x)y=0,a≤x≤b

with the Robin (mixed) boundary conditions

α1y(a)+β1y′(a)=0,α2y(b)+β2y′(b)=0 where P and Q are continuous on [a,b], and αi and βi are real constants such that (αi,βi)≠(0,0). Furthermore, suppose the fundamental solutions to the equation are y1(x) and y2(x).

Now, let's define the following matrix:

A=[α1y1(a)+β1y1′(a)α1y2(a)+β1y2′(a)α2y1(b)+β2y1′(b)α2y2(b)+β2y2′(b)]

Then, the BVP has a unique, trivial solution y≡0 if and only if det(A)≠0.

In other words, if the determinant equals zero, then the BVP has infinitely many solutions.

Notice that, in our case, we have Neumann boundary conditions. So, setting αi=0,βi=1,a=0, and b=π, the matrix A reduces to

A=[y1′(0)y2′(0)y1′(π)y2′(π)].

To find the fundamental solutions, we set y=emx. The auxiliary equation is m2+4=0. So, we have m=±2i. So, the fundamental solutions are y1(x)=cos⁡2x and y2(x)=sin⁡2x. Differentiating, we have y1′(x)=−2sin⁡2x,y2′(x)=2cos⁡2x.

Therefore, the matrix A is A=[−2sin⁡(2⋅0)2cos⁡(2⋅0)−2sin⁡(2⋅π)2cos⁡(2⋅π)]=[0202]

and we have det(A)=0⋅2−2⋅0=0.

Since det(A)=0 we conclude that this BVP has infinitely many solutions.
